content: Coenzyme Q, also known as ubiquinone, facilitates the translocation of protons across a lipid bilayer, specifically the inner mitochondrial membrane in the case of mitochondria. This process is integral to the biochemical generation of ATP. The modified Q cycle in Complex III involves a series of redox reactions. During this process, cytochrome c is oxidized, ubiquinol (QH2) is reduced to ubiquinone (Q), and four protons are translocated into the intermembrane space for every two cycles of the reaction. Ubiquinol binds to the Qo site of Complex III through hydrogen bonding interactions with His181 of the Rieske iron-sulfur protein and Glu272 of cytochrome b. Ubiquinone, on the other hand, binds to the Qi site of Complex III. Ubiquinol undergoes a bifurcated oxidation, donating one electron to the Rieske iron-sulfur protein (FeS protein) and another to the bL heme. This oxidation produces a transient semiquinone intermediate before complete oxidation to ubiquinone, which then dissociates from the Qo site. The FeS protein, having accepted an electron from ubiquinol, becomes free to migrate to the cytochrome c1 subunit. It subsequently donates its electron to cytochrome c1, reducing its heme group. The electron is then transferred to an oxidized molecule of cytochrome c, which is externally bound to Complex III. This reduced cytochrome c dissociates from the complex and continues in the electron transport chain. Additionally, the reoxidation of the FeS protein releases a proton bound to His181 into the intermembrane space. The second electron from ubiquinol, transferred to the bL heme, is used to reduce the bH heme. The bH heme then transfers this electron to the ubiquinone bound at the Qi site, reducing it to a semiquinone radical. A proton taken up by Glu272 is transferred to a hydrogen-bonded water chain as Glu272 rotates 170° to form a hydrogen bond with a water molecule, which is in turn hydrogen-bonded to a propionate group of the bL heme. This step leaves a stable semiquinone at the Qi site, indicating that the reaction is not yet complete. A second Q cycle is required to complete the process. During this second cycle, the second electron transferred from cytochrome bH reduces the semiquinone to ubiquinol. The final products of the Q cycle are four protons translocated into the intermembrane space, two protons taken up from the mitochondrial matrix, and the reduction of two molecules of cytochrome c. The reduced cytochrome c is eventually reoxidized by Complex IV in the electron transport chain. This process is cyclic, as the ubiquinone generated at the Qi site can be reused by binding to the Qo site of Complex III, thus perpetuating the cycle.
